title: Measurement Types
text:
Gain (similar to voltage on certain cytometers) is an unit which detected signal is amplified by for each detector. An instrument applies different gains to each detector, allowing for use of dim and bright fluorophores. During the Daily QC, these gains normally get minor adjustments to keep the QC beads’ signal constant, allowing for comparison of .fcs files acquired on different days. As the individual lasers in the cytometer are used, they slowly wear down and more gain is applied to remain at that setpoint. This contributes to the slowly increasing view typical of the gain plots:





Generally, when a laser is begining to rapidly wear out, we see steeper increases in the Gain plots. When the field service engineer replaces the laser, the gain values are reset according to the new laser. In this example, you can see that pattern for the violet laser of the instrument was replaced twice (red lines indicating field service engineer visit):





For the Cytek instruments, a Daily QC fail is triggered when the Gain is >100% of the original baseline Gain value. When this happens, a red flag is added to that timepoint. We have observed that .fcs files acquired on gain spike days (as seen below) may still have altered unmixing even if they have not exceeded the >100% threshold, so it’s worth keeping an eye on.








The robust coefficient of variation (rCV) is a measure of the resolution between the positive and negative population for each detector. When the value is high, dim staining populations may be harder to distinguish from the negative population. For spectral instruments where entire spectrum is used to identify a fluorophore, increased rCV on the detector where a fluorophore has its main peak has impacted unmixing for users with larger panels (>20 fluorophores). The RCV plots will typically resemble the following:





For Cytek instruments, a Daily QC fail is only triggered when %rCV exceeds either 8% for SSC, or 6% for FSC and the following detectors: UV3, V3, B3, YG3, R3. When this happens, the instrument will appear as failed on the home page:





When we navigate to the History tab and find that date, we can see that the rCV for UV3 failed, which was what triggered the QC fail:





But what happens if the RCV fails on any of the other detectors (UV1-> UV2, UV4 -> UV16,etc.)? Since they are not the indicator detectors, they won’t trigger a Cytek QC fail. However, since we have observed unmixing issues when the RCVs of these other detectors are exceeded, we don’t want to ignore them. Consequently, when a non-indicator RCV fails, we show it as failed under the Daily View:





And label the instrument as caution for that given day:





How to interpret these Caution notices depends on what we see in the Levey-Jennings plots. For a few detectors (especially UV1/UV2), they exceed the 6% cutoff but are stable over time. Consequently, the impact of the increased RCV is relatively minimal.





By contrast, is the RCV went from consistently stable, to spiking, the impact on your unmixing is likely to be significantly greater.

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text: Secondary QC for the Cytek Aurora EVO from SPHERO URCP-38-2K Ultra Rainbow beads. The set resolves into 6 populations — blank particles (peak 1) plus 5 fluorescent rainbow levels (peaks 2–6). Note on the Aurora: daily QC adjusts each APD’s gain to pin bead MFI to a target, so raw MFI is held ~constant by design — the informative signals are the ones gain can’t compensate: sensitivity (2+2SD limit of resolution, Q & B), %CV, and linearity. Heavy FCS processing is done once by scripts/Process6PeakUltra.R; this page reads the peak_metrics.csv archive (+ the daily-QC gain) so it stays light.

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Peak clustering






NotePeak clustering — cluster images and cluster sizes (click to expand)





The 6 URCP-38-2K populations are assigned once per run by model-based clustering (flowClust, K = 6) on the asinh-transformed anchor detectors, then read out in every detector. This is far more robust than per-detector peak finding: weak channels can’t resolve dim peaks alone, but the strong anchor detectors can, and a bead’s population label is fixed across all detectors. Labels are ordered 1–6 by ascending brightness: peak 1 = blank particles, peaks 2–6 = fluorescent rainbow levels. Clustering runs in Process6PeakUltra.R; this page reads the persisted result.

2D cluster assignment (V8-A × B9-A)
The per-run diagnostic: each run’s gated beads shown on two detectors that both resolve all 6 peaks. A clean assignment shows 6 tight, ordered, single-coloured blobs along the diagonal — blank (peak 1) at the dim end, brightest (peak 6) at the top — with no interleaving.

Code
clus_imgs <- sort(list.files("images/6peak_ultra_evo", pattern = "^cluster2d_.*[.]png$", full.names = TRUE))
if (length(clus_imgs) == 0) cat("_No saved cluster images yet — run `scripts/Process6PeakUltra.R`._\n\n") else {
  cat("::: {layout-ncol=3}\n")
  for (f in clus_imgs) cat(sprintf("![Run %s](../%s)\n\n", sub("^cluster2d_(.*)[.]png$","\\1",basename(f)), f))
  cat(":::\n")
}

Cluster-size sanity
URCP-38-2K mixes the 6 populations in roughly equal proportions (blank particles may be slightly more abundant). Cluster sizes should be broadly even — a quick numeric check that no population was split or merged by the clustering step.


Code
csz <- pm |> group_by(run_label, peak) |>
  summarise(events = mean(n, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(peak = factor(peak, levels = 1:n_peaks))
gp(ggplot(csz, aes(factor(peak), events, fill = run_label,
                   text = sprintf("peak %s | %s<br>mean events %.0f", peak, run_label, events))) +
     geom_col(position = position_dodge()) +
     labs(title = "Cluster size per peak (events per run; peak 1 = blank)",
          x = "Peak", y = "Events", fill = NULL) +
     theme_bw(base_size = 10), 300)

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Tracking over time
Peak-6 median intensity and %rCV per laser across runs. A stable row means stable performance; a step or drift flags a laser problem. In-range peaks only.

Per-laser overview
Two 5-laser × run heatmaps of peak-6 deviation from each detector’s baseline (first run), averaged across the laser. Top: median intensity shift (blue = dimmer, red = brighter). Bottom: %rCV shift (blue = tighter, red = broader). A whole-row shift points to a laser-level issue; an isolated tile flags a single detector.


Code
p6_base <- pm |> filter(peak == n_peaks, in_range) |> group_by(detector) |>
  slice_min(run_label, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  transmute(detector, base_median = median) |> ungroup()
laser_delta <- pm |> filter(peak == n_peaks, in_range) |>
  left_join(p6_base, by = "detector") |>
  mutate(delta_pct = (median - base_median) / base_median * 100,
         laser = factor(laser_of(detector), levels = laser_levels)) |>
  group_by(laser, run_label) |> summarise(delta_pct = mean(delta_pct, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
lim <- max(abs(laser_delta$delta_pct), na.rm = TRUE); if (!is.finite(lim) || lim == 0) lim <- 1
gp(ggplot(laser_delta, aes(run_label, laser, fill = delta_pct,
        text = sprintf("%s laser | %s<br>%+.1f%% vs baseline", laser, run_label, delta_pct))) +
     geom_tile(colour = "white") +
     scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(laser_levels)) +
     scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0,
                          limits = c(-lim, lim), name = "Peak 6\nΔ median\nvs t0") +
     labs(title = "Per-laser peak-6 median deviation from baseline", x = NULL, y = "Laser") +
     theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10)), 420)








Code
p6_base_cv <- pm |> filter(peak == n_peaks, in_range) |> group_by(detector) |>
  slice_min(run_label, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  transmute(detector, base_rcv = rcv) |> ungroup()
laser_delta_cv <- pm |> filter(peak == n_peaks, in_range) |>
  left_join(p6_base_cv, by = "detector") |>
  mutate(delta_pct = (rcv - base_rcv) / base_rcv * 100,
         laser = factor(laser_of(detector), levels = laser_levels)) |>
  group_by(laser, run_label) |> summarise(delta_pct = mean(delta_pct, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
lim_cv <- max(abs(laser_delta_cv$delta_pct), na.rm = TRUE); if (!is.finite(lim_cv) || lim_cv == 0) lim_cv <- 1
gp(ggplot(laser_delta_cv, aes(run_label, laser, fill = delta_pct,
        text = sprintf("%s laser | %s<br>%+.1f%% vs baseline rCV", laser, run_label, delta_pct))) +
     geom_tile(colour = "white") +
     scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(laser_levels)) +
     scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0,
                          limits = c(-lim_cv, lim_cv), name = "Peak 6\nΔ %rCV\nvs t0") +
     labs(title = "Per-laser peak-6 %rCV deviation from baseline", x = NULL, y = "Laser") +
     theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10)), 420)

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
%CV & noise floor
Peak 6 (brightest) uses robust %CV — it has a well-defined mean (~1–2% when healthy). The blank (peak 1) uses its absolute robust spread (IQR/1.349), not %CV: the blank sits near zero, so %CV explodes when the mean dips toward zero even though the actual spread is unchanged. A rising blank spread is a genuine noise-floor increase.


Code
gp(heat(cvtop, "cvt", "Peak-6 %CV", "brightest population (mean well-defined)"))

























Code
gp(heat(cvp1, "sd1", "Peak-1 noise floor", "absolute robust spread (IQR/1.349), not %%CV"))
gp(heat_fc(cvp1, "sd1", "Noise floor — fold-change", "lower is better; red = noisier than its best", higher_better = FALSE))























































Code
cl_lat <- cvtop |> group_by(laser = factor(laser_of(detector), levels = laser_levels), run_label) |>
  summarise(cvt = mean(cvt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
gp(ggplot(cl_lat, aes(run_label, cvt, colour = laser, group = laser)) +
     geom_line() + geom_point() +
     labs(title = "Mean peak-6 %%CV per laser (± control context as runs accumulate)",
          x = NULL, y = "Peak-6 %%CV") + theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
     theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)), 320)

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Brightest peak (peak 6) %CV
A focused per-detector view of peak 6 (the brightest fluorescent level) alone over time. The brightest population is normally the tightest (~1–2%), so any rise is a sensitive indicator of saturation, noise, or linearity issues at the top of the dynamic range. The cross-detector snapshot and per-laser mean are under %CV & noise floor.






NotePeak-6 %CV trend per detector (expand — one panel per detector)







Code
peak6 <- pm |> filter(peak == n_peaks, in_range)
ggplot(peak6, aes(run_label, rcv, group = detector)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") + geom_point(size = 1, colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ detector, scales = "free_y", ncol = 6) +
  cv_y_scale +
  labs(title = "Peak-6 robust %%CV over time (brightest URCP-38-2K level)",
       x = NULL, y = "Peak-6 %%CV") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 5, angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Sensitivity (2+2SD, Q & B)






New method (2026-11-11). Sensitivity now uses the Parks 2017 weighted quadratic fit and the Parks 2018 2+2SD limit of resolution, adopted from the cross-instrument Sensitivity study. The previous CV²-vs-1/x / STN-17 version is archived in _attic/6peak_ultra_v1_2026-11-11/.



The headline metric is the 2+2SD limit of resolution: the smallest amount of dye whose −2 SD edge clears the blank’s +2 SD edge. Lower = more sensitive. It combines detection efficiency (Q) and the background noise floor (BSD) into one number, which is why Parks et al. (2018) recommend it for tracking and comparing instruments. On this EVO the limit is background-limited (the photon 4/Q share is typically 2–5%), so it is mostly driven by blank noise and is stable run to run (~5–10%).
It is calculated for all 64 detectors in as-acquired MFI. Daily QC pins bead MFI to fixed targets, so the MFI scale is held constant (the URCP MEF-per-MFI factor k moves ~2% across all runs, including the v2-gain change). A detector that loses sensitivity therefore shows up as a higher limit at the pinned scale. For the 18 detectors with a URCP-38-2K certificate assignment it is also reported in MEF below.






NoteMethod & provenance — read me





Per detector and run, the variance of each bead population (raw MFI) is fit as
V = c0 + c1·M + c2·M²
on all non-saturated peaks, including the blank (Parks et al., Cytometry A 2017;91:232), by weighted least squares with weights n / (2·V̂²), iterated to convergence. c0 is background variance, c1·M photon (shot) noise, c2·M² the intensity-proportional spread (bead intrinsic CV + illumination). Per-peak SD is IQR/1.349; for the blank the right-half SD (P84 − P50) is used (Chase & Hoffman 1998), and SDs are used directly — never %rCV × median, which flips sign when a blank median is ≤ 0.








Quantity
Formula
Units




2+2SD (all detectors)
4·(c1 + blank SD)
MFI


2+2SD (MEF detectors)
4·(1/Q + BSD)
MEF


Q
k / c1 (MEF) · gain / c1 (relative, all detectors)
Spe per MEF · relative


B
c0 / (c1·k) (MEF) · c0 / c1² (all detectors)
MEF · Spe


BSD
measured blank SD / k (checked against fitted √c0 / k, within ~5%)
MEF


CV₀
√c2
%


k
slope-1 log–log fit of median vs certificate MEF, peaks 2–6
MFI per MEF



Validity. Fits with χ²/df > 50 (weighted residuals vs pure sampling noise; 2–7 is normal with IQR-based SDs) are suppressed, since the model does not describe the data (listed in the table below). When the fit is fine but its photon term is swamped by blank noise and bead CV on the dim peaks, Q’s own fit SE exceeds 100% and Q = 1/c1 can jump 10–100× (e.g. V4-A on 2026-07-06 13:54 and 2026-11-05). Those Q and B values are suppressed as unresolved, and the 2+2SD is kept, since it is ~95% blank-driven. For MEF values the free log–log slope must be 0.9–1.1 with R² > 0.98; otherwise the certificate’s MEF scale does not match that detector (most UV and violet channels here, slopes 1.15–1.36; PE-Cy5 0.79). Those rows are still shown, flagged as lower-confidence.
Caveats. Q is a statistical-photoelectron Q: it includes APD multiplication noise, so it is not a quantum efficiency, and with only ~500–1,000 events per peak its per-run fit SE is ~30% — read Q and B as relative trends. Red detectors (APC, APC-Cy7) are lower-confidence because the dim beads’ intrinsic CV is large there (Hoffman & Wood 2007). Each value is for one raw detector, not sensitivity after unmixing. Full derivation: Sensitivity Articles/QB_2plus2SD_method_summary.md.

if (fc_locked) cat(sprintf("> **FC reference: LOCKED** to qualified window %s – %s (per-detector median ± SD).\n",

  cat(sprintf("> **FC reference: dynamic / preliminary** — each detector vs its own best of %d run(s). Lock a fixed reference once enough qualified runs accumulate.\n", n_runs))


FC reference: dynamic / preliminary — each detector vs its own best of 27 run(s). Lock a fixed reference once enough qualified runs accumulate.

# Absolute limits differ by orders of magnitude between detectors, so aggregate the
# per-detector % change from baseline (comparable across detectors) per laser.

  mutate(laser = factor(laser_of(detector), levels = laser_levels)) |>
  group_by(laser, run_label) |> summarise(d = median(lor_mfi_d, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
gp(ggplot(ll, aes(run_label, d, colour = laser, group = laser,
                  text = sprintf("%s laser | %s<br>median Δ 2+2SD %+.1f%% vs baseline", laser, run_label, d))) +
     geom_line() + geom_point() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
     labs(title = "Median 2+2SD change from baseline per laser (up = less sensitive)",
          x = NULL, y = "2+2SD change vs baseline (%)") +
     theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)), 320)

'Q unresolved' rows (Q fit SE > 100%) keep their 2+2SD but show blank Q and B tiles. 'c2<0' / 'c0<0' rows keep their 2+2SD but have CV₀ fixed at 0 or B undefined.")
}

Q & B (relative, all detectors)
Q and B from the same fit, in statistical-photoelectron terms: Q = gain / c1 (relative detection efficiency, higher = better), B = c0 / c1² (background in photoelectrons, lower = better). Both divide by the fitted photon term c1, which is the least precise coefficient (~30% SE per run), so expect more run-to-run scatter here than in the 2+2SD limit and look for sustained shifts rather than single points.

Linearity
MEF-calibrated (SPHERO URCP-38-2K) for the 18 certificate detectors, plus a rank-based R² overview for all 64. On the log–log fit a slope ≠ 1 means the detector does not match the certificate’s MEF assignment (spectral mismatch); curvature flags compression or saturation (bright end) or floor effects (dim end). The certificate’s 5 fluorescent peaks map directly to data peaks 2–6 (peak 1 = blank, unassigned).
